idiom_name: tuple deconstruction swap ((a, b) = (b, a)) over a single state reference
implementation_notes: The classic structure has no C# analogue and is not needed: there is no user-defined copy/move, no ADL and no noexcept, and reference assignment can neither allocate nor fail, so a type that keeps its representation behind one reference field commits a new state by rebinding that field. For exchanging two variables the language itself provides the operation - C# 7 tuple deconstruction, (a, b) = (b, a), which the compiler lowers to plain loads and stores without materialising a ValueTuple - and for shared state System.Threading.Interlocked.Exchange(ref location, value) performs the exchange atomically. Keep the fallible work (constructing the new State) before the assignment; the pattern's remaining rules are about what you swap (one reference, not a set of fields) rather than about how.
pitfalls: Property setters, indexers and user-defined Deconstruct/implicit conversions run user code: an exchange routed through a property can throw or validate, so swap backing fields when the commit must not fail.

Interlocked.Exchange<T> is atomic for a single location only (and before .NET 9 T had to be a reference type); swapping two independent fields or two atomic cells is not atomic and can be observed torn.
readonly fields, init-only properties and positional record members cannot be exchanged after construction - which is often the right answer: replace the whole object instead of swapping its parts.
Swapping two structs copies their bytes (tuple deconstruction of structs included), so bulk state belongs behind a class reference to keep the exchange O(1).
